newsitem.title: PERU: Explosions shatter peace at Peru siege site.
newsitem.headline: Explosions shatter peace at Peru siege site.

text.p: Two explosions were heard early on Tuesday at the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima, briefly shattering the stillness surrounding the compound, witnesses said.

Two loud booms, possibly gunshots, rang out at around 4:00 a.m. local time (0900 GMT) and were immediately followed by silence, police and witnesses said. There were no signs of movement at the residence, where Marxist guerrillas have been holding 74 hostages for three weeks.
"It sounded like two gunshots," a police officer patrolling a block away from the diplomatic compound told Reuters. There were no reports of injuries, he said, adding, "We're investigating."

Reuters Television images filmed from a vantage point above the residence showed a man, dressed in combat gear and carrying an automatic rifle, running across the driveway at the front of the compound shortly before the explosions.
Immediately following the explosions police surrounding the residence moved into a state of alert but did not approach the building, witnesses said.
Another police officer at the site said later he was certain that the explosions had not been caused by police.
They were the first explosions heard at the residence since Dec. 26 when a single loud explosion briefly shook the area.

The explosions underscored the delicately balanced nature of the crisis, which started 21 days ago when about 20 heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels stormed a coktail party at the residence and took more than 500 guests hostage.

President Alberto Fujimori, who has maintained a "no compromises" position throughout the siege, met late into the night with ministers to discuss options for bringing about a peaceful end to the crisis, Government Palace sources said. The meeting lasted for nearly 10 hours, the sources said.
Fujimori has rejected rebel demands that he free about 400 of their comrades who are imprisoned in harsh conditions.
In a hard-hitting speech on Thursday, Fujimori called the MRTA "terrorists" bent on pointless violence that served to increase poverty in Peru.
The rebels have not freed any hostages since that speech and an MRTA spokesman said on Monday they would continue to hold firm until the two sides sat down to negotiate.

"There will be no more releases so long as the government fails to agree to a political solution," Isaac Velazco, the MRTA's international spokesman, said in a telephone interview from Hamburg, Germany.

He said a "political solution" would consist of Fujimori sending Education Minister Domingo Palermo for further talks inside the residence and allowing rebels to communicate with their imprisoned comrades.

Palermo, Fujimori's chief negotiator, held face-to-face negotiations with the MRTA on Dec. 28. The meeting was followed by the release of 20 hostages and a conciliatory rebel statement expressing willingness "to withdraw from the occupied residence by way of dialogue."
But Palermo has not been sent back to the residence, and the rebels have hardened their position.
"We have made too many gestures. We have released many people without receiving a single response from the government," Velazco said.
The series of hostage releases -- in which the guerrillas freed a total of more than 430 captives -- has stopped since seven men were let out on New Year's Day.
The impasse has sparked fears that one false move by the government or rebels could trigger a bloody showdown.
In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto warned on Monday that the situation could get out of hand.
"It will be a protracted battle, and situations like that make me worried about an unexpected accident," he told reporters.
The rebels, who are known to possess automatic rifles and grenade launchers, have mined and booby-trapped the residence in anticipation of any assault by government forces.
